title: IELTS Listening Chuyên Sâu: 6 Minute English - Fraud
description: Bài học IELTS Listening chuyên sâu giúp học viên nâng cao vốn từ vựng học thuật và kỹ năng nghe hiểu qua chủ đề 'Fraud' (Tội phạm gian lận tài chính).
transcript:
Sam: Hello I’m Sam and welcome to 6 Minute English. This is the programme where in just six minutes we discuss an interesting topic and teach some related English vocabulary. Joining me to do this is Rob.

Rob: Hello. And today we’re talking about ___fraud___.

Sam: Fraud is the criminal activity of getting money by ___deceiving___ people – or tricking people by doing something dishonest.

Rob: There are many ways to do this – and much of it is happening ___online___ these days.

Sam: We’ll talk more about this in a moment. But first, a very honest quiz question for you to answer, Rob. According to UK Finance – an organisation that ___represent___ the British banking ___industry___ – how much money did criminals steal through fraud and scams last year? Was it…. a) £1.2m, b) £120m, or c) £1.2bn

Rob: Well, I imagine it’s quite a lot – so I’ll say £120m.

Sam: We'll find out if you're right later in the programme. Now, I just mentioned the word '___scam___', which is an illegal way of making money by tricking someone. We may think that we’ll never be scammed, but already millions of people have ___fallen for___ fake emails, phone calls or letters that look ___genuine___ and ask us to give or update our ___financial___ details.

Rob: To fall for means to believe something that is a trick or a lie, to be true. This year, for example, thousands of people in the UK fell for a ___fraudulent___ – or fake – email, requesting that people update their direct debit details for paying their TV licence. That's a payment we have to make in the UK to fund the BBC.

Sam: This is something the BBC Radio 4 programme, You and Yours, has been discussing. Its BBC Fraud ___investigator___ reporter, Shari Vahl, explained why it was easy to be deceived…

Shari Vahl: It's a ___sleight of hand___ fraud. Criminals get you to look over there whilst they ___rifle___ your pockets and I have the email here and it looks completely ___convincing___. All the right logos, all the right ___fonts___. It just says that my direct debit on my TV licence has failed and I need to pay it. It’s very polite.

Sam: So some great language there. She said that this scam was a sleight of hand fraud. 'Sleight of hand' means the use of clever skill to gain something dishonestly – in this case, money.

Rob: As Shari said, the criminals get you to, metaphorically, look over there whilst they rifle your pockets. 'Rifle' means search something in order to steal from it– so to steal from your pocket – very dishonest!

Sam: Now, like in this case, ___fraudsters___ – the people who commit fraud – gained financial information by '___phishing___'. That’s not fishing using a rod, line and hook, but by sending an email that looked like it came from your bank, asking for ___confidential___ information.

Rob: But banks do warn us not to give away our financial details online and to change our ___passwords___ regularly.

Sam: But sometimes criminals are very clever in what they do and it’s easy to be fooled. The You and Yours programme also heard about this from social engineer, Jenny Radcliffe. What does she call this type of fraud?

Jenny Radcliffe: The more ___sophisticated___ frauds are ones that have been thought through very carefully. And this has been thought through. It’s a fraud that can be ___layered___ so you know we're getting some information from you. What you really look for is a ___window___ into someone - a key that unlocks just a small part of their ___identity___ or their personal data and from that a good fraud will build and build and build on it until the consequences to some people can be completely ___devastating___.

Rob: So Jenny Radcliffe is talking about 'sophisticated' fraud. That means it’s clever and often complicated – so it can confuse us.

Sam: Yes, criminals need just a small piece of information about us – a key – that can eventually open up our identity and ___expose___ our personal data.

Rob: And as Jenny says, for victims of fraud the consequences – the outcome – can be very bad. Especially if somebody loses all their hard-earned savings – it can be devastating.

Sam: Of course banks and ___security___ companies are working hard to beat the criminals but it still remains a problem and earlier I asked you, Rob. According to UK Finance, how much money did criminals steal through fraud and scams last year?

Rob: I said b) £120m. That’s a lot of money.

Sam: It is but it’s even more. In 2018, criminals successfully stole £1.2 billion through fraud and scams – and that’s just in the UK – ___globally___ it’s even more.

Rob: Well, it certainly is a serious issue but hopefully we haven’t deceived you with the vocabulary we’ve discussed today.

Sam: Hopefully not! We’ve been talking about fraud – that’s the ___criminal___ activity of getting money by deceiving people – or ___tricking___ people by doing something dishonest.

Rob: Next we had 'scam' - which is an illegal or dishonest way of making money by tricking someone. The people who do it are '___scammers___'.

Sam: We talked about the phrasal verb 'fall for'...

vocabulary.meaning: Sự lừa đảo, tội phạm gian lận tài chính
vocabulary.example: He was convicted of bank fraud.

vocabulary.meaning: Lừa dối, gạt ai đó
vocabulary.example: Don't try to deceive me with false promises.

vocabulary.meaning: Trò lừa đảo (thường trực tuyến/qua điện thoại)
vocabulary.example: He lost his life savings in a telephone scam.

vocabulary.meaning: Bị mắc bẫy, tin vào lời lừa dối
vocabulary.example: Millions of people have fallen for fake emails.

vocabulary.meaning: Mang tính lừa lọc, gian lận
vocabulary.example: They made a fraudulent claim on their insurance.

vocabulary.meaning: Có sức thuyết phục, nhìn rất thật
vocabulary.example: The fake website looked remarkably convincing.

vocabulary.meaning: Mánh xảo quyệt, thủ thuật nhanh tay lẹ mắt
vocabulary.example: It was a clever sleight of hand fraud that tricked everyone.

vocabulary.meaning: Lục lọi, tìm kiếm nhanh để trộm đồ
vocabulary.example: The thief rifled through her purse while she wasn't looking.

vocabulary.meaning: Kẻ gian lận, kẻ lừa đảo
vocabulary.example: Fraudsters are using sophisticated technology to steal passwords.

vocabulary.meaning: Lừa đảo qua email/mạng để lấy thông tin cá nhân
vocabulary.example: Phishing scams often ask for your banking passwords.

vocabulary.meaning: Bảo mật, bí mật
vocabulary.example: Never share your confidential financial details online.

vocabulary.meaning: Tinh vi, phức tạp, công phu
vocabulary.example: Cybercriminals use increasingly sophisticated techniques.

vocabulary.meaning: Nhiều tầng, nhiều lớp phức tạp
vocabulary.example: It's a layered fraud that builds over time.

vocabulary.meaning: Danh tính, thông tin cá nhân
vocabulary.example: Identity theft is a growing concern worldwide.

vocabulary.meaning: Mang tính tàn phá, hủy hoại hoàn toàn
vocabulary.example: Losing all savings can have a devastating impact on victims.

vocabulary.meaning: Thật, chính hãng, không phải giả
vocabulary.example: Make sure you only reply to genuine emails from your bank.

vocabulary.meaning: Nạn nhân
vocabulary.example: The scam left many victims financially ruined.

vocabulary.meaning: Phơi bày, làm lộ ra
vocabulary.example: The leak exposed personal data to hackers.

vocabulary.meaning: Hậu quả, kết quả
vocabulary.example: You must accept the consequences of sharing passwords.

vocabulary.meaning: Trích nợ tự động qua tài khoản ngân hàng
vocabulary.example: I set up a direct debit to pay my monthly bills.

mcqQuestions.q: "Criminals get you to look over there whilst they rifle your pockets." What does this metaphor mean?
options: Criminals use physical force to steal from your clothes while you are distracted.
Criminals distract your attention with something else while secretly stealing your money.
Criminals ask you to look at a map while they clean your pockets.
Criminals help you find lost items in your pocket.

mcqQuestions.q: "It's a sleight of hand fraud." What does the speaker imply?
options: The fraud requires physical magic tricks.
The fraud uses clever skill and deception to trick victims without them noticing immediately.
The fraud is easy to detect if you look closely at your hands.
The fraud only happens during live stage performances.

mcqQuestions.q: "All the right logos, all the right fonts. It just says that my direct debit on my TV licence has failed..." Why was the scam email so effective?
options: Because it was sent directly from the official BBC office.
Because it demanded a very large sum of money immediately.
Because its visual presentation perfectly mimicked an official, legitimate email.
Because it contained spelling errors that made people feel sorry for the sender.

mcqQuestions.q: "What you really look for is a window into someone - a key that unlocks just a small part of their identity..." What does "a window into someone" represent here?
options: A literal glass window in a victim's home.
A small piece of personal information that gives fraudsters access to further exploit the victim.
A software application installed on a computer screen.
An open conversation about a person's physical health.

mcqQuestions.q: "...and from that a good fraud will build and build and build on it until the consequences to some people can be completely devastating." What is the main idea of this statement?
options: Frauds usually stop once criminals get a tiny piece of information.
Fraudsters start small and gradually use gathered information to cause ruinous harm to the victim.
Fraud building takes many years and rarely affects victims financially.
Victims can easily rebuild their lost assets after a fraud occurs.

mcqQuestions.q: "To fall for means to believe something that is a trick or a lie, to be true." How can this phrase be rephrased in context?
options: To be physically injured by a scammer.
To accidentally drop your bank details on the floor.
To be tricked into believing a deception.
To fall in love with someone who works in a bank.

mcqQuestions.q: "That’s not fishing using a rod, line and hook, but by sending an email that looked like it came from your bank..." How does the speaker define 'phishing'?
options: A outdoor sport done near rivers using internet connection.
Fraudulently impersonating a trusted institution via email to steal confidential data.
Buying fish online using a stolen credit card.
Catching cyber-criminals using special software.

mcqQuestions.q: "The more sophisticated frauds are ones that have been thought through very carefully." What characterizes a 'sophisticated fraud'?
options: It is simple, fast, and easy for anyone to notice.
It is meticulously planned, elaborate, and difficult to detect.
It is executed by young people using basic mobile phones.
It only targets large multi-national corporations.

mcqQuestions.q: "Banks do warn us not to give away our financial details online and to change our passwords regularly." What action is advised by banks?
options: Sharing passwords with family members for safety.
Keeping confidential details private and updating passwords systematically.
Changing bank accounts every few months.
Writing passwords down on paper letters.

mcqQuestions.q: "In 2018, criminals successfully stole £1.2 billion through fraud and scams – and that’s just in the UK – globally it’s even more." What does this statistical highlight demonstrate?
options: Fraud is a minor financial issue confined to small towns.
UK banks lost money because of internal banking mistakes.
Fraud is a massive, high-impact problem with worldwide scale.
Most scams in 2018 were successfully prevented by UK Finance.
